notes.short: Prudence to the simple, knowledge to the young
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. The simple, easily led to good or evil, answer the young, who have no experience yet; prudence answers knowledge and discretion, the wariness that escapes evil and finds good.

lines.words: To impart prudence to the simple
and knowledge and discretion to the young,

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) takes the simple as one easily led to good or evil, a sense the parallel line bears out with the young man, one without experience; he treats prudence and discretion alike, as qualities that here mean wariness to escape evil and find good.
notes.limit: The note claims only that the two lines answer each other in sense, not that the simple and the young are one and the same group.

cites.quote: simple--one easily led to good or evil; so the parallel. young man--one inexperienced. subtilty--or prudence ( Pro 3:21 ; Pro 5:21 ). discretion--literally, "device," both qualities, either good or bad, according to their use. Here good, as they imply wariness by which to escape evil and find good.

notes.short: Proverbs and parables, sayings and riddles
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: proverbs and parables, then the sayings and riddles of the wise. The word rendered parables is an obscure saying that needs interpreting, so it answers the riddles of the second line.

lines.words: by understanding the proverbs and parables,
the sayings and riddles of the wise.

original.note: In Hebrew the word rendered parables (melitsah) is an obscure saying that needs interpreting, and the riddles (chidah) are knotted, intricate sayings.

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes) says that rendering the word as interpretation spoils the parallel of the two clauses, and that riddle or enigma better gives its meaning. J. W. Nutt (Ellicott's Commentary) takes it as an obscure thing that needs interpreting, and so answering the dark sayings, which he calls literally knots, intricate sayings.

cites.quote: The rendering "interpretation" spoils the parallelism of the two clauses, and fails to express the Hebrew. In Hab 2:6 , it is rendered "taunting proverb." Here "riddle" or "enigma" would better express the meaning.

notes.short: Swallowed like Sheol, gone down into the Pit
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. The Pit of the second line is another name for Sheol in the first, the deep place of the dead. The sinners boast that they will devour their victims as Sheol does, as suddenly as those who go down into the Pit.

lines.words: let us swallow them alive like Sheol,
and whole like those descending into the Pit.

original.note: In Hebrew Sheol (she'ol) and the Pit (bor) are two names here for the depth where the dead go.

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes) reads the two lines as one boast, all-devouring as Sheol and sudden as the going down into the pit, and calls the Pit here a synonym for Sheol, the great depth, the world of the dead.
notes.limit: Some render the second line of the upright, who are made like those who go down to the Pit; the note follows the BSB.

notes.evidence: E. W. Bullinger (Figures of Speech Used in the Bible) sets these lines out as an introverted parallel: your destruction, your fear, your fear, your destruction, the first line answering the fourth and the second the third.

notes.short: Wrong gain, righteousness; then righteous, wicked

but righteousness brings deliverance from death.
The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry,
but He denies the craving of the wicked.

but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him.

favor is better than silver and gold.

notes.short: Poverty comes on the slacker “like a robber”
notes.about: The slacker is sent to learn from the ant, which gathers its food in season with no one to drive it. If he keeps on sleeping, poverty will come upon him like a robber, and need like a bandit. It comes on him surely, and he has no defence against it.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit
figure.means: want that comes surely on the idle man while he sleeps, and that he cannot withstand

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes) says the similitude is drawn from two Eastern terrors, the thief and the armed robber, and sloth is more destructive than both. Henry says want will come step by step, as one that travels, and irresistibly, like an armed man. Clarke and J. W. Nutt (Ellicott) explain the two pictures: poverty draws near surely, and the sleeper cannot withstand it.
notes.limit: Older renderings call the robber one who travels, and the writers differ on that picture: one who draws steadily nearer, or a thief who comes suddenly or swiftly. Each way, the poverty comes surely.

cites.quote: The similitude is drawn from the two sources of Eastern terror: the "traveler," i. e., "the thief in the night," coming suddenly to plunder; the "armed man," literally "the man of the shield," the armed robber. The habit of indolence is more fatally destructive than these marauders.

notes.short: Six things, seven, and then the list
notes.about: A number is given, then a greater one, and then the list follows line by line in the same build: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a scheming heart, feet quick to evil, a false witness, and one who stirs up discord.

lines.words: There are six things that the LORD hates,
seven that are detestable to Him:
haughty eyes,
a lying tongue,
hands that shed innocent blood,
a heart that devises wicked schemes,
feet that run swiftly to evil,
a false witness who gives false testimony,
and one who stirs up discord among brothers.

notes.evidence: Lowth says that where a set number is given twice over for an open one, the list of particulars that follows naturally makes the lines parallel, of the synthetic kind and no other; he gives these verses as an example of it.

cites.quote: Of the same sort of Parallelism are those passages, frequent in the Poetic Books, where a Definite number is twice put for an Indefinite; this being followed by an enumeration of particulars naturally throws the sentences into a Parallelism, which cannot be of any other than the Synthetic kind. ... notes.short: Two warnings of loss: your goods, then your life
notes.about: The two lines are not set against each other; both warn of what this sin costs a man, and the loss is double. The first line says it brings him down to poverty; the second says the adulteress hunts his very life.

lines.words: For the levy of the prostitute is poverty,
and the adulteress preys upon your very life.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line says a man is brought down to a loaf of bread (kikkar lechem), a mark of poverty; the second says she hunts a precious life (nefesh yeqarah).

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the parallelism synonymous, not antithetic: the man who takes this course is doubly threatened with loss, squandering his means to poverty and having his precious soul made a prey.
notes.limit: Some, following the Greek translation, set the lines against each other: the prostitute costs a man only a loaf of bread, but the adulteress hunts his life.

cites.quote: the parallelism is synonymous, not antithetic: he is doubly threatened with loss who enters upon such a course. notes.short: Wisdom prepares a feast and invites the simple
notes.about: Wisdom builds her house, prepares her meat and wine, and sends out her maidservants to call the simple to her table. The picture runs on to her call: “Leave your folly behind, and you will live.” Some of the writers set it beside Jesus' parables of a great feast.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.means: the good things Wisdom offers all who lack judgment, food for mind and heart, pictured as a rich feast she has made ready and calls them to share

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it an allegorical picture of a present reality rather than a parable, its flesh and wine figures of food for mind and heart. Joseph Benson calls it an allegory that Jesus' parables of the feast illustrate. Matthew Henry says Wisdom's provision is shown under the similitude of a feast. E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes) and Adam Clarke call it a parable.
notes.limit: Some of these writers call it a parable. They differ on what the house stands for: heaven or the church in one reading, the world God made in another.

cites.quote: If we had a parable before us, the perf. would have run into the historical ... but it is ... an allegorical picture of the arrangement and carrying out of a present reality. ... Since the figure is allegorical, we may not dispense with the interpretation of the number seven ... figure.words: The woman named Folly is loud

Matthew Henry takes the woman to mean carnal pleasure, and her guests in Sheol to be those under the power of sin.

but a foolish son grief to his mother.

notes.short: Blessings on the righteous, violence with the wicked
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: blessings rest on the head of the righteous, but violence goes with the mouth of the wicked. Head answers mouth, and righteous answers wicked.

lines.words: Blessings are on the head of the righteous,
but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.

original.note: In Hebrew the verb of the second line means to cover, so it can be read as the mouth of the wicked hiding violence, or as the violence he has done covering his mouth, falling back on him.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the verse an antithetic distich and reads violence as covering the mouth of the wicked, which he says keeps the contrast sharp. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) takes blessings as praises and reads the mouth of the wicked as hiding violence, so it has no praises. Adam Clarke sets the shame that covers the wicked against the blessings on the just.
notes.limit: Writers differ on the second line: some read it as the mouth of the wicked hiding violence, others as the violence he has done coming back to cover his own mouth.

notes.short: His hope dies with him, even hope in his strength

and the hope of his strength vanishes.

notes.short: The simple inherit folly; the prudent wear a crown
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: the simple and the prudent, folly and knowledge. Folly comes to the simple as their lot, but the prudent gain knowledge and wear it like a crown.

lines.words: The simple inherit folly,
but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.

original.note: In Hebrew the verb for crowned answers the verb for inherit and goes beyond it: what is inherited simply comes to a man, while knowledge worn as a crown is a possession won.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the verb for crowned the parallel word to inherit and a heightening of it, and says the prudent, on the contrary, gain knowledge as a crown, a possession won and not merely an inheritance. J. W. Nutt (Ellicott's Commentary) sets the simple, who become self-willed, against the prudent, whom knowledge adorns as a crown.

cites.quote: As a parallel word to נחלוּ, יכתּרוּ ... since in the relation to נחלו one expects an idea surpassing this ... folly is their possession, i.e., their property. but envy rots the bones.

notes.limit: The cited writers take the verse both of bodily health and of the inner, moral life.

and how good is a timely word!

notes.short: Wicked thoughts detested, pure words pleasing
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. What the LORD detests, the thoughts of the wicked, is set against what pleases Him, the words of the pure. Thoughts are paired with words, for words come from the thoughts behind them.

lines.words: The LORD detests the thoughts of the wicked,
but the words of the pure are pleasant to Him.

notes.about: Read with the fear of the LORD as its subject, the two lines are built alike: the fear of the LORD is the schooling that leads to wisdom, and humility is the road that leads to honor. The way up to honor goes through lowliness.

lines.words: The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom,
and humility comes before honor.

notes.short: Deep waters, then a bubbling brook of wisdom
notes.about: The second line carries on the first instead of setting anything against it. The words of a man's mouth are deep waters, not easily sounded; they are also a fountain of wisdom, a brook that keeps bubbling up fresh.

the fountain of wisdom is a bubbling brook.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verse is neither antithetic nor synonymous but one statement over two lines: three things are said of a man's words, that they are deep waters, a bubbling brook and a fountain of wisdom. notes.limit: Not all read it so: some take the two lines as a contrast between the dark depths of a man's words and the clear brook of wisdom.

notes.short: Many companions may ruin; one friend stays close

lines.words: A man of many companions may come to ruin,
but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line's word for companions is a general one, while the second line calls the true friend one who loves.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the antithetical second line calls the true friend by a word for one who loves, against the general word for companions, and that one such friend is better than many. E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes): not the multitude of so-called friends, but the one whose love is stronger than kinship. E. W. Bullinger sets the many friends against the one faithful friend.

notes.short: Food for her household, portions for her maids
notes.about: The last two lines answer each other: food for her household, and portions for her maidservants. Because the portions stand beside the food, they can be read as the maids' fixed share of food, which she gives out early while most of the house still sleeps.

lines.words: to provide food for her household
and portions for her maidservants.

original.note: In Hebrew the word rendered portions means a fixed, allotted share; it can also mean an appointed task, but set beside food it reads as a share of food.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the word for portions can mean the day's appointed work, but the parallel with food points to a fixed portion of food, and that she herself gives out the day's food early, while most of the house is still asleep.
notes.limit: Some take the portions as each maidservant's task for the day rather than her share of food.
